sense: in earnest, not joking; of a person, grave

terms.gloss: serious, earnest (of things said or done)
terms.grammar: adjective; as a noun, sēria, serious matters
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.134: sī sēriīs, sevēritātem adhibeat, sī jocōsīs, lepōrem
Hor. S. 1.1.27: āmōtō quaerāmus sēria lūdō
terms.comment: The opposite of jocōsus: in jest or in earnest, jocō an sēriō. Classical writers use it only of things; of a person they say sevērus (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; later Liv., Quint.; not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short)
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 541: Jocōne an sēriō illaec dīcat, nesciō
Traupman 107, 376: sēriōne dīcis tū?, are you serious?
terms.comment: A favourite word of Plautus. Vērōn' sēriō?, “Really? Seriously?”

terms.gloss: serious, grave, stern (of a person or a face)
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.228: omnium gravissimus et sevērissimus (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 2.289: vultus sevērior et trīstior (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also strict and severe: the same word serves for a serious face and a stern father.

terms.gloss: serious, dignified, weighty (of a person: the opposite of levis)
evidence: Cic. Lael. 95: inter … levem cīvem, et inter cōnstantem et vērum et gravem

phrases.latin: sed tamen āmōtō quaerāmus sēria lūdō
phrases.english: but still, joking aside, let us look into serious things

phrases.latin: Jocōne an sēriō illaec dīcat, nesciō
phrases.english: whether he says that in jest or in earnest, I don’t know

phrases.latin: lūdō autem et jocō ūtī illō quidem licet, sed sīcut somnō et quiētibus cēterīs tum, cum gravibus sēriīsque rēbus satis fēcerimus
phrases.english: we may indeed enjoy play and joking, but, like sleep and other rest, only when we have done what serious and weighty matters require

sources: Lewis & Short: serius · Lewis & Short: severus · Lewis & Short: gravis
